name: Iris Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior administrator at a small family accountancy firm, twelve of us, above a shoe shop on the high street. I book client appointments, chase people for their receipts before the tax deadline, keep the files in order and run the post. I still keep a paper desk diary next to the computer, because I trust it. The best part is when a nervous client leaves calmer than they arrived because I found their missing paperwork.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: January. Everyone leaves their tax returns until the last fortnight, and the phone doesn't stop. Last January I worked three Saturdays in a row, and Tomas, my partner, said he'd forgotten what I looked like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that new things are mostly oversold. At work I'd tell the partners we were right not to rush into buying anything. With friends I'd shrug and say good, one less thing to worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but not completely settled. Mr Kaplan, the senior partner, is sixty-eight and keeps talking about selling the firm to a bigger chain. A bigger chain would have its own admin team in a city office, and I don't know where that leaves me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job well, because that's what keeps you employed. I'd keep the three months' savings topped up and maybe add a bit after Tomas's overtime. I'd also start quietly looking at what other firms nearby pay, just to know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not because of AI, just because the firm's future isn't settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How likely do you think the sale is?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say even chances in the next three years. Mr Kaplan's son doesn't want to take over, he's an engineer. If a chain buys us, they'll keep the accountants and the clients and probably not much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Tomas cut if your pay stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our weekend trips to the coast, first. Then probably the second phone contract and the gym I barely use. Tomas drives buses for the council, so his pay is steady, but it doesn't cover the rent on its own.

say: I'd say new things are mostly **oversold**, and we were right not to rush.
With friends I'd shrug and call it **one less worry**.
think: The senior partner may **sell the firm** to a chain, which threatens my job anyway.
A chain would run admin from a **city office**, so AI isn't my only risk.
do: Keep doing the job **well** and keep three months' **savings** topped up.
Quietly check what **other firms** nearby pay.
S0.quote: A bigger chain would have its own admin team in a city office, and I don't know where that leaves me.
fieldNote: Her worry in this picture is the **firm sale**, not technology.
She trusts **paper** and doing the job well as her protection.
Her partner Tomas's **steady pay** doesn't cover the rent alone, so her income matters.

steps.text: Keep the three months' savings topped up from Tomas's overtime
Check what other accountancy firms nearby pay admin staff
Keep running the January rush the same way as always

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to use these things where they help, but someone still has to check it all. I wouldn't say much online, I don't really post. At work I'd ask the partners to bring it in slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one scares me. Booking, checking and answering clients is my whole day, and I've never touched these tools. If the firm gets an AI that chases receipts and books appointments, they'd keep one admin, and the young one, Chloe, already uses the stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go on whatever course the partners offer, even though I'd hate it. I'd put more aside each month, maybe a hundred and fifty, and cut the coast trips. I'd also update my CV, because I haven't touched it in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm good at this job, but in the wrong way for what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Chloe already uses the tools. How do you feel about her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like her, she's bright, and she's twenty-two. I trained her on the filing myself. It'd be odd to be pushed out by someone I taught, but I wouldn't blame her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. Firms have to cut costs or they lose clients to the chains. I'd just want them to be honest with me early.

say: I'd say use the tools where they help, but **someone must check** it all.
At work I'd ask the partners to bring it in **slowly**.
think: Booking, checking and answering clients is **my whole day**, and I've never used AI.
They'd keep **one admin**, and the younger one already uses the tools.
do: Go on whatever **course** the partners offer, despite hating it.
Save an extra **hundred and fifty** a month and cut the coast trips.
Update her **CV** for the first time in five years.
feel: **Anxious** that she's good at the job in the **wrong way**.
S1.quote: I'm good at this job, but in the wrong way for what's coming.
fieldNote: She blames **nobody**, seeing cuts as normal business, which fits her centre outlook.
Being replaced by a **colleague she trained** stings quietly.
She'd learn the tools only because she feels **cornered**.

steps.text: Sign up for the partners' AI course despite disliking it
Save an extra hundred and fifty a month
Update her CV for the first time in five years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to sort out some kind of support quickly, because people can't adapt in two years. I'm not one for protests, but I'd vote for whoever had a clear plan. At work I'd keep quiet and keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm finished in admin by 2028. Accountancy is all thinking work, so the whole firm shrinks, not just me. The robots coming three years later don't help someone who sits at a desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking straight away at jobs where you use your hands or deal with people face to face. Maybe the pharmacy counter, or training as a dental receptionist, though that's still admin. Tomas and I would stop saving for a wedding and put it all into the emergency pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd be lying awake running numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Tomas's job in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He drives a bus, so the robots would come for that around 2031. That's three years more than me. So for a while his wage would be what keeps us going, which is a strange thought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a wedding. What would happen to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd put it off. We'd planned for next summer, small, at his mum's church hall. I'd rather be married without a party than spend the savings on a party when I've no job.

say: I'd say government must **sort out support** quickly, since two years is too short.
I'd **vote** for whoever had a clear plan but keep quiet at work.
think: I'm **finished in admin** by 2028, because accountancy is all thinking work.
The **robot delay** doesn't help someone who sits at a desk.
do: Look straight away for **hands-on** or face-to-face work, like a pharmacy counter.
Stop the **wedding savings** and move everything into the emergency pot.
S2.quote: I'd rather be married without a party than spend the savings on a party when I've no job.
fieldNote: She understands that **Tomas's driving job** outlasts hers by about three years.
Her move to a **pharmacy counter** shows she's thinking about people-facing work.
Postponing the **wedding** is the clearest sign of how seriously she takes this.

steps.text: Apply for pharmacy counter or face-to-face reception jobs
Postpone next summer's wedding at the church hall
Move the wedding savings into the emergency pot
Vote for the party with a clear plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but it's something, and I'd want employers and government to use it properly. At work I'd ask what the firm's plan is. I'd be calmer in public than I feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd still expect to lose this job by 2031. Five years gives me time to change, but I'm slow to change, and I know it. I'd probably leave it too long, hoping it wasn't true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself do something in the first year, probably an evening course in pharmacy assistant work. I'd keep the job at the firm while I study. We'd still have the wedding, but smaller, and we'd keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but with a sliver of a plan. It's the waiting that would get me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why pharmacy rather than something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My aunt Leila runs a pharmacy in the next town and always says she can't find good staff. It's people, it's careful work, and it's partly hands-on. Robots would take longer to do that than my filing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd leave it too long. What would make you act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Kaplan telling us a date, probably. Once there's a date, I'd move, but without one, I'd keep telling myself next year.

say: I'd say five years is **short but something**, and should be used properly.
At work I'd ask the firm what its **plan** is.
think: I'd still expect to **lose this job** by 2031.
I'm **slow to change** and might leave it too long.
do: Start an evening **pharmacy assistant** course in the first year.
Keep the firm job while studying and have a **smaller wedding**.
feel: **Alarmed**, with only a sliver of a plan; the **waiting** is the worst part.
S3.quote: Once there's a date, I'd move, but without one, I'd keep telling myself next year.
fieldNote: She knows her **resistance** could cost her the head start.
Her aunt's **pharmacy** gives her a concrete, local option.
She needs an **outside deadline** to act.

steps.text: Enrol on an evening pharmacy assistant course
Keep working at the firm while studying
Scale the wedding down to a small one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough if people are sensible and don't panic. I'd tell friends to start thinking about it, but not to rush. At work I'd probably go along with whatever the firm brings in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a relief compared with the others, but the job still goes. I'd be thirty-seven, and I could have a new trade by then. The question is whether I actually start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go and spend a few Saturdays at my aunt's pharmacy to see if I like it. If I do, I'd start the course within two years. We'd have the wedding as planned, and I'd keep saving the extra each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a slow anxious. Ten years of warning feels like a bill due in a year: you know it's coming and you still put it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI at the firm in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, eventually, when the partners bring it in. I'd let Chloe show me. I'd never be the first, but I'd rather learn it than be shown the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything about the ten years that gives you hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That Tomas and I could plan it together without panic. We'd sit down at the kitchen table with a pad and work out the years. That's how I like to do things.

say: I'd say ten years is enough if people **don't panic**.
I'd tell friends to start thinking but **not rush**.
think: It's a **relief** compared with the others, but the job still goes.
The question is whether I **actually start** changing.
do: Spend a few **Saturdays** at her aunt's pharmacy to test the work.
Start the **course** within two years if she likes it.
Have the **wedding** as planned and keep saving the extra each month.
feel: A **slow anxious**, like a bill due in a year.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning feels like a bill due in a year: you know it's coming and you still put it off.
fieldNote: She likes planning at the **kitchen table**, which suits a decade's warning.
Even with time, she doubts her own **willingness to start**.
She'd learn AI from a **younger colleague**, reluctantly.

steps.text: Work a few Saturdays at her aunt's pharmacy to try it
Hold the wedding next summer as planned
Keep saving the extra hundred and fifty each month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years isn't enough for someone like me who takes a year to decide anything. What would help is some kind of steady income while people retrain, and employers telling you early instead of at the last minute.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'd talk to my family about it. I don't think I would, not at first. My parents would worry, and they've got enough on.

headlineQuote: I still keep a paper desk diary next to the computer, because I trust it.
portrait: Iris is a **27-year-old** senior administrator at a small family **accountancy firm**, loyal to her paper diary.
She's **centre** in her views, blames nobody, and sees cuts as **normal business**.
She's **resistant** to new tech and admits she might leave it **too long** to change.
She's **uneasy** even in AI Plateau because the firm may be **sold**, and alarmed under faster AGI.
Her partner **Tomas** drives a bus, and their **wedding** plans shift with each picture.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she takes a year to **decide** anything.
whatWouldHelp: A **steady income** while retraining, and employers giving **early warning**.
